Zap
ZAP
verb / interjection (Boomer slang)
Imitative, the sound of a ray gun or an electric jolt, first popularized in science-fiction comics (the Buck Rogers strip, from 1929). As a verb, to zap — to kill or destroy with a sudden blast, then to hit, defeat, or jolt — is mid-twentieth century; the 1960s gave it countercultural flair (Robert Crumb’s Zap Comix, 1968), and the 1970s–80s added zap in the microwave and zapping channels with a remote. Zapped also means exhausted.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To zap is to hit something with a sudden blast — a ray gun in a comic book, a bug in an electric trap, leftovers in the microwave, an enemy in a video game. It is the sound of instant, effortless destruction, and the Boomer generation grew up imagining it on Saturday-morning cartoons. The Christian observation: Scripture records a moment when two disciples wanted to zap their enemies, and the Lord’s answer is one of the most important rebukes in the Gospels. A Samaritan village refused to receive Jesus, and "when his disciples James and John saw this, they said, Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did? But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. For the Son of man is not come to destroy men’s lives, but to save them" (Luk 9:54–56). The zapping instinct — wipe out the people who annoy or oppose us — is the opposite of the gospel. God’s judgment is real and will come as suddenly as lightning: "as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be" (Mat 24:27). But the reason it has not yet come is mercy: "The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance" (2Pe 3:9). Our children play games in which enemies are zapped by the hundred. A father can enjoy the game with them and still teach Luk 9:56: the Son of man came to save.

Webster 1828 Definition

Imitative comic-book word (1929; mid-20th-c. verb) for destroying with a sudden blast, later to microwave, to channel-surf, or to exhaust — the instinct James and John showed in Luk 9:54, which the Lord rebuked: "the Son of man is not come to destroy men’s lives, but to save them" (Luk 9:56).

ZAP, v.t. (mid-20th c.; Boomer-era slang) 1. To destroy or kill with a sudden blast, as of a ray gun. 2. To strike or jolt suddenly. 3. To cook or heat in a microwave oven (1970s–). 4. To change channels with a remote control (1980s). interj. The sound of such a blast. Zapped, adj., exhausted.

Imitative; first popularized in science-fiction comic strips (Buck Rogers, 1929).

Decode for families: video games are built on the zap. Teach the verse that rebukes it.

Key Scripture

Luk 9:54 — "And when his disciples James and John saw this, they said, Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did?"

Luk 9:55 — "But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of."

Luk 9:56 — "For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them. And they went to another village."

Mat 24:27 — "For as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be."

2Pe 3:9 — "The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance."

Modern Corruption

The zap imagines effortless, instant destruction of whatever annoys us; Christ rebuked that spirit in His own disciples and delays His sure judgment out of longsuffering mercy.

expand to see more

Comic books and cartoons taught a generation to imagine power as the ability to blast an enemy instantly and without cost. Video games have perfected it. There is nothing wrong with a child’s game of pretend, but the imagination it trains can leak into real life — the wish to zap the rival, the critic, the irritating neighbor, the other political party. James and John, the "sons of thunder," had that wish, and they even had a biblical precedent in Elijah. Jesus rebuked them anyway: "Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of" (Luk 9:55).

The gospel’s power is the opposite of the zap. It is slow, patient, and costly: the Lord bore the fire Himself rather than calling it down on others. The judgment will come, sudden as lightning (Mat 24:27); until then, God’s patience is salvation (2Pe 3:9). A Christian who has been spared the fire he deserved will be slow to call it down on anyone else.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Imitative zap (ray-gun sound) → 1929 Buck Rogers comics → mid-20th-c. verb (to blast) → 1968 Zap Comix → 1970s–80s microwave and remote-control senses.
